title: Indian Passport Fees Jump Up to 75% From July 1. Here’s What Changes for NRIs.
excerpt: The Ministry of External Affairs has revised passport charges across the board — fresh applications, renewals, Tatkaal, and replacements all cost more. With 32 million overseas Indians, the timing is hard to ignore.
body:
Starting July 1, every Indian passport application will cost significantly more. The Ministry of External Affairs notified the Passports (Amendment) Rules, 2026, on June 20, replacing the fee schedule that had been in effect under the Passports Rules, 1980. The increases range from 43 percent for Tatkaal services to 75 percent for standard 60-page booklets — the steepest single revision in recent memory.

## What’s Changing

The new fee structure hits every category of applicant:

**Adults (18 and above):**
- Fresh or reissued 36-page passport: ₹1,500 → ₹2,500 (67% increase)
- Fresh or reissued 60-page passport: ₹2,000 → ₹3,500 (75% increase)
- Tatkaal 36-page: ₹3,500 → ₹5,000
- Tatkaal 60-page: ₹4,000 → ₹6,000
- Lost or damaged replacement (36-page): ₹5,000 (normal), ₹7,500 (Tatkaal)
- Lost or damaged replacement (60-page): ₹6,000 (normal), ₹8,500 (Tatkaal)

**Minors (under 18):**
- Fresh passport (36 pages): ₹1,750 (normal), ₹4,250 (Tatkaal)
- Lost or damaged replacement: ₹4,250 (normal), ₹6,750 (Tatkaal)

Children under eight and senior citizens over 60 will receive a 10 percent discount, but only on fresh passport applications — not on reissues or renewals.

Passport validity remains unchanged: 10 years for adults, and five years or until the applicant turns 18 (whichever is earlier) for minors.

## What Hasn’t Changed

The revised rules do not alter the application process itself. Applications will continue to be filed through the Passport Seva portal and processed at Passport Seva Kendras (PSKs) and Post Office Passport Seva Kendras (POPSKs) across the country. The chip-enabled e-passport programme, which has been gradually rolled out since 2021, also continues as planned.

Indian missions and consulates abroad will apply the same revised fee structure for overseas applications. NRIs renewing or applying through Indian embassies should expect local processing surcharges on top of the base revision.

## Why It Matters for NRIs

India has one of the world’s largest diaspora populations — over 32 million Non-Resident Indians and Persons of Indian Origin spread across every continent, according to the Ministry of External Affairs. For this community, the passport is not just a travel document; it is the single most important link to citizenship, property rights, inheritance claims, and visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to over 60 countries.

The fee increase arrives at a time when passport demand is rising. India issued over 13 million passports in the last financial year, with a significant share of renewals driven by the Gulf diaspora — where Indian passports must be renewed every 10 years to maintain residency permits in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, and Oman. For families with multiple members, the cumulative increase is substantial: a family of four renewing 60-page passports will now pay ₹14,000 in application fees alone, up from ₹8,000.

## Part of a Broader July 1 Overhaul

The passport fee revision is one of several financial changes taking effect on July 1, 2026. The new Income Tax Act, 2025 — which replaced the 1961 law — extends the ITR filing deadline for certain categories to August 31, and revised returns can now be filed until March 31 of the following year.

Banks are now required to report credit card spending exceeding ₹10 lakh in a financial year to the Income Tax Department. Personal expenses on company-issued credit cards will be treated as taxable perquisites — a change that could affect NRIs who maintain Indian corporate credit cards.

## The Bottom Line

If you have a passport renewal due in the next few months, the math is straightforward: applications submitted before July 1 will be processed at the current, lower fee. The revised rules apply to all applications received on or after that date. With the increase amounting to ₹1,000–1,500 per passport for most applicants, procrastination has a price.

For the 32 million Indians abroad, the fee hike is a minor inconvenience in isolation. But combined with rising consular service costs, tighter documentation requirements for OCI cardholders, and the ongoing complexities of dual-tax compliance, it is one more reminder that the bureaucratic cost of being Indian abroad keeps quietly climbing.
